title: The Half-Life of Board Expertise
author: Marianna Zangrillo
summary: Zangrillo and Keil challenge the governance assumption that seasoning compounds. Their argument is that director expertise now behaves less like financial capital and more like a depreciating asset, because AI, geopolitical realignment, new regulation and shifting business models shorten the shelf life of hard-won knowledge. They name this the half-life of board expertise and draw a staffing conclusion that goes beyond simply refreshing boards more often. The proposal is to stop treating every seat as identical: hold a stable core of directors who carry institutional memory and strategic context, and deliberately create seats whose value is time-bound and tied to a specific strategic challenge. A Partners Group example shows the approach in practice, with a brand specialist recruited for a two year repositioning and the succession communicated from the outset so that the handover produced no bad blood. The closing move elevates curiosity to a governance capability, arguing that how quickly a board updates its assumptions now matters as much as the experience it already holds.
points: The authors reframe director experience as a depreciating rather than a compounding asset, and give the depreciation a name.
Their fix is not faster board turnover but differentiated seats, with some directors carrying continuity and others recruited for time-bound expertise.
The Partners Group rebranding example shows a planned two year director tenure announced in advance so the exit is not read as a failure.
Boards are told to ask how fast they update assumptions, not only whether the skills matrix looks complete.
Curiosity is elevated from a personal trait to a governance capability, alongside the board's willingness to admit what it does not know.
quotes: For decades, boards have treated experience as a competitive advantage. The underlying assumption has been simple: the more seasoned the directors, the better the board's judgement. But what if that assumption no longer holds?
Artificial intelligence, geopolitical shifts, new regulation and rapidly evolving business models mean that expertise acquired over a successful career can become outdated surprisingly quickly.
We call this the half-life of board expertise: the time it takes for the strategic relevance of a board's collective knowledge to diminish.

The challenge is therefore not to choose between stability and renewal, but to combine them deliberately. Boards still need directors who understand the company's history, culture and strategic context.
Not every board seat needs to serve the same purpose. Some directors provide continuity. Others contribute expertise that is valuable precisely because it is time-bound.

Rather than focusing only on whether they have the right mix of skills and experience, they should also ask how quickly they update their assumptions, expose themselves to new ideas and recognise when long-held beliefs no longer fit reality.
The most effective boards of the future may not be those with the deepest reservoir of experience, but those that recognise when experience is no longer enough.
